quote: P’rsnally, I would say that John is committing a type error, like trying to subtract 5 grams from 20 meters. “The morning star” is not the same type as the morning star, let alone the same thing. Beliefs are not planets.
content: This is Frege’s own solution to Frege’s own puzzle. “Über Sinn und Bedeutung” (1892) introduced the morning star and evening star to argue that in belief contexts an expression refers not to its customary referent but to its customary sense, so that substitution of co-referring names fails there for a principled reason; Quine’s “referential opacity” (Quine (1956)) is the same diagnosis for quotation and attitude contexts. The essay presents this as a personal view offered against philosophers who are “still arguing,” and what the philosophers are still arguing about is the residue that the type distinction leaves. Kripke’s puzzle about belief (“A Puzzle about Belief,” 1979, a book chapter with no DOI) is the decisive case: Pierre, raised in France, believes “Londres est jolie”; he later moves to an ugly part of London, learns English directly, and comes to believe “London is not pretty,” never realizing the names co-refer. No substitution of terms has been performed by anyone, quote marks change nothing, and Pierre appears to hold contradictory beliefs while being perfectly rational. The type error diagnosis handles the case the essay describes; it does not handle the case that kept the argument going, which is why the argument kept going.

quote: Alfred Tarski once tried to define the meaning of “true” using an infinite family of sentences:
content: Tarski did not “try” this and it was not his definition. The T-sentences are Convention T, his adequacy condition on any definition of truth for a language; the definition itself is recursive, via satisfaction, and one of its results is that truth for a language cannot be defined within that language (Tarski (1944)). The essay then reads Tarski as vindicating correspondence: “Saying ‘true’ compares a belief to reality.” Tarski explicitly declined to take sides on that (he said his conception was “neutral” between correspondence, coherence and pragmatist accounts), and the leading modern use of his schema is the opposite of the essay’s. Deflationists argue that the T-sentences exhaust the content of “true,” so that there is no relation of comparison to reality to be analysed at all (Horwich, Truth, 1990; Field (1994)). The essay’s advice, to notice when the T-sentences start seeming meaningful, is good advice; what one is then in a position to see is that they are compatible with both the essay’s theory of truth and its main rival, and settle nothing between them.
